1.pericope_label: Lord, remember David, and all his afflictions: how he sware unto the Lord... Until I find out a place for the Lord, an habitation for the mighty God of Jacob

schools.summary: Delitzsch makes the speaker the post-Davidic church and defines both the idiom of remembering and the verbal noun behind 'afflictions'; Ellicott derives that word from a verb meaning to declare and renders it 'declarations'.
Gill leaves the speaker open between David and Solomon and reads the vow as hyperbole; Calvin surveys the authorship question at length and blocks the inference to intercession of the dead.
Clarke assigns the psalm to the close of the captivity and the second temple, and gives David's resolve a practical shape.
Henry reads the psalm as Solomon's dedication address pleading his father's vow; Spurgeon presses the paradox of praying for what God has already sworn.

debates.question: Who wrote the psalm, and when?

positions.summary: Probably an inspired author at the close of the captivity, referring to the second temple; David is proposed without sufficient ground, Solomon with more likelihood.

Most likely Solomon, since the whole tenor is an exact epitome of his dedication prayer and the closing sentences are identical with three verses here — though the third-person mention of David tells against David's own authorship.
The speaker is the post-Davidic church reminding God of the mercies with which he answered David's trouble.
Solomon, addressing God at his own dedication and pleading his father's vow rather than his own merit.

debates.question: What are the 'afflictions' God is asked to remember?

positions.summary: Not afflictions at all: the word is the plural infinitive of a verb meaning to declare, so read 'all his declarations'.
The care and trouble David took in procuring a worthy abode for the sanctuary, the verb meaning to harass oneself about something.
Either all the troubles of his life, which his anointing occasioned, or his uneasiness that the ark was in curtains — some rendering it his meekness.

outliers.summary: Uses the verse to refuse the argument for intercession of the dead: the faithful are not calling an advocate from the tomb but appealing to the covenant God made with David, which though given to one man was to be communicated to all.
Presses the paradox that what we are assured God will do must nevertheless be made a matter of prayer, since he swears precisely that our faith may have confidence.

themes: Lord, remember David, and all his afflictions:
How he sware unto the Lord, and vowed unto the mighty God of Jacob;
Surely I will not come into the tabernacle of my house, nor go up into my bed;
I will not give sleep to mine eyes, or slumber to mine eyelids,
Until I find out a place for the Lord, an habitation for the mighty God of Jacob.

6.pericope_label: Lo, we heard of it at Ephratah: we found it in the fields of the wood... turn not away the face of thine anointed

schools.summary: Ellicott identifies Ephratah with Bethlehem on the strength of Genesis, Ruth and Micah, corrects 'tabernacles' to 'habitation', and reads the closing plea as an intercession for a later prince.
Gill takes Ephratah for the tribe of Ephraim, reads the tabernacles of the churches among the Gentiles, and refuses to ground the last plea on David's merit.
Clarke offers two constructions of the Ephratah verse, the second putting the words in the mouth of the captives in Babylon; Wesley identifies the city of woods and the footstool.
Spurgeon dwells on why the ark deserved to be called the ark of strength, and on the condition that the Lord must rest with it.

debates.question: Where are Ephratah and the fields of the wood?

positions.summary: Ephratah is Bethlehem, as Genesis, Ruth and Micah require, David's purpose being naturally connected with his family's birthplace; the fields of the wood is Kirjath-jearim.
Ephratah is the tribe of Ephraim, where the ark stood at Shiloh — a tribe God did not choose; the city of woods is Kirjath-jearim.
Either a continuation of David's vow, or, more plainly, the words of the captives in Babylon rehearsing the ark's history and praying for the ruined city.

debates.question: Does the seventh verse look back or forward?

positions.summary: Forward: it expresses a present determination rather than recalling the past, since David's project has given this generation a place of worship — true even if the psalm is post-exilic.
Spiritually forward, of the churches raised among the Gentiles as Christ's dwelling places.

debates.question: On whose behalf is the closing plea made?

positions.summary: By the people at large for one of David's successors — in Chronicles Solomon prays for himself, but here an Asmonean prince is in view; the phrase 'turn away the face' is borrowed from court etiquette.
By the anointed for himself, asking not to be cast out of God's presence.
Not on David's merit at all, but for the sake of the covenant and of the antitypical David in whose name prayers are presented.

outliers.summary: Explains the title 'ark of thy strength' from the ark's own history: in captivity it smote its captors and broke their gods, and when brought back it guarded its honour by the death of those who treated it with disrespect.
Notes that 'ark of thy strength' occurs nowhere else but in one other psalm, where 'strength' alone denotes the ark, and that the technical word for ark occurs nowhere else in the psalms.

themes: Lo, we heard of it at Ephratah: we found it in the fields of the wood.
We will go into his tabernacles: we will worship at his footstool.
Arise, O Lord, into thy rest; thou, and the ark of thy strength.
Let thy priests be clothed with righteousness; and let thy saints shout for joy.
For thy servant David’s sake turn not away the face of thine anointed.

11.pericope_label: The Lord hath sworn in truth unto David; he will not turn from it... His enemies will I clothe with shame: but upon himself shall his crown flourish

schools.summary: Delitzsch lists the sanctuaries Zion displaced and traces the order of the blessings; Ellicott renders the oath clause, dates the horn image, and prefers 'I have trimmed a lamp'.
Gill separates the absolute promise to the Messiah from the conditional one to David's seed, and reads horn, lamp and shame messianically.

Clarke states the failure of the condition and the transfer to the true David, and makes the largest claim in the chapter for the finality of the Christian dispensation; Wesley glosses the lamp and the priests' clothing.
Henry sets God's oath against David's and makes the Zion promises as applicable to the gospel church as the Davidic ones to Christ; Spurgeon rests everything on the immutability of the oath.

debates.question: How should the oath clause be rendered?

positions.summary: Not 'in truth' but as a comment on the oath itself: it is a true oath, he will not depart from it.
By his truth, as elsewhere he swears by his holiness — or possibly 'hath sworn truth unto David'.

debates.question: What is the 'rest for ever' that God chooses?

positions.summary: Not Mount Zion nor the temple, since 'for ever' cannot apply to them, but the church, in whom God rests and abides.
The Christian church indubitably: after it there never will be another dispensation, Christianity closing all communications from heaven to earth.
Zion as against Shiloh, Bethel, Mizpah, Kirjath-jearim and the house of Obed-Edom, each of which held the ark only for a season.
Both at once: the promises about Zion's hill are as applicable to the gospel church as those about David's seed are to Christ.

debates.question: What are the horn and the lamp?

positions.summary: The Messiah: the Targum's glorious King, the horn figured from the horns of cattle, the budding pointing to the name Branch.

A sprouting horn as an image of vigorous life, with the messianic application drawn out in Zechariah's song; and 'I have trimmed a lamp', the verb being that used of the sacred lights under Aaron's charge.
A successor to continue for ever in the family, and particularly one eminent light.
The power and authority of the spiritual David in the Christian church, and a posterity secured.

outliers.summary: Sets the two oaths against each other — David swore to find God a house, so God swore to build David one — on the principle that God will be behind with none of his people.
Divides the promise itself: the first part absolute and respecting the Messiah, the second conditional and relating to David's seed, whose observance of the law was the condition of the kingdom.

themes: The Lord hath sworn in truth unto David; he will not turn from it; Of the fruit of thy body will I set upon thy throne.
If thy children will keep my covenant and my testimony that I shall teach them, their children shall also sit upon thy throne for evermore.
For the Lord hath chosen Zion; he hath desired it for his habitation.
This is my rest for ever: here will I dwell; for I have desired it.
I will abundantly bless her provision: I will satisfy her poor with bread.
I will also clothe her priests with salvation: and her saints shall shout aloud for joy.
There will I make the horn of David to bud: I have ordained a lamp for mine anointed.
His enemies will I clothe with shame: but upon himself shall his crown flourish.
